<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:lifting}
Let \(k\) be any field.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The isomorphism classes of \(\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}(k)\) are the \(k^\times\)-orbits on \(k^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\) for the weighted action.
\item Every \(k\)-point of the coarse variety \(\mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w}\) has a representative in \(k^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\).
\item The orbits lying over a coarse \(k\)-point of support \(S\) form a torsor under \(H^1(k,\mu_{k_S})\simeq k^\times/(k^\times)^{k_S}\): if \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\) is one representative, the others are, up to the action of \(k^\times\), the vectors \((a^{w_i/k_S}\tilde x_i)_i\) with \(a\in k^\times\).
\end{enumerate}
The same holds for a closed substack \(\mathfrak X\subset\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}\) defined by weighted homogeneous equations and its coarse space \(X\).
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
An object of \(\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}(k)\) is a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsor over \(\operatorname{Spec} k\) with an equivariant map to \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\). Hilbert's Theorem 90 gives \(H^1(k,\mathbb{G}_m)=0\), proving (i). Parts (ii) and (iii) are \cite[Lem.~2.1, Prop.~3.7]{paper-1}. Their proofs use only this vanishing and the fppf Kummer sequence for \(\mu_{k_S}\), so they apply over any field. For a substack, the cone is stable under the weighted action; hence every representative of a point of \(X\) lies on it.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:twists}
Let \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) have support \(S\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(\mathbf{x}\) has a representative in \(\hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\{0\}\), and every \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\)-representative of \(\mathbf{x}\) lies on \(\hat X\);
\item the \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times\)-orbits of \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\)-representatives of \(\mathbf{x}\), that is, the twists lying over \(\mathbf{x}\), form a torsor under \(H^1(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}},\mu_{k_S})\); there are \(g_S(r)\) of them, each orbit has \((q^r-1)/g_S(r)\) elements, and each twist \(\xi\) has \(\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})=\mu_{k_S}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), of order \(g_S(r)\);
\item consequently
\[
\#\bigl(\hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\{0\}\bigr) = (q^r-1)\,|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|,
\qquad
\#\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})) = \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})} g_{S(\mathbf{x})}(r).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Parts (i) and (ii) are \cref{lem:lifting} for \(k=\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\), where \(\#H^1(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}},\mu_{k_S})=g_S(r)\) and the stabilizer of a vector of support \(S\) in \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times\) is \(\mu_{k_S}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\). Part (iii) follows by summing over \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
The \textbf{degree-based weighted height} is
\[
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}) := r_\mathbf{x} \cdot \min_{\lambda \in \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times} \max_{0\leq i\leq n} \frac{\deg(\lambda^{w_i} x_i)}{w_i}.
\]
Since the denominators \(w_i\) are fixed, the inner maximum takes values in a discrete subset of \(\frac1m\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), where \(m=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathbf{w})\); hence the minimum is attained.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
We set \(\deg(0)=1\).  This convention keeps every term in the maximum positive and will be used throughout this subsection.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{Pp1}
The function \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}\) satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item (Finiteness) For any \(B>0\), the set \(\{\mathbf{x}\in X(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)\mid H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\) is finite.
\item (Weighted scaling) If \(\mathbf{x}\sim\lambda\cdot\mathbf{x}\), then \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})=H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\lambda\cdot\mathbf{x})\).
\item (Functoriality of field of definition) If \(\phi:X\to Y\) is a morphism of weighted varieties defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), then \(r_{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\leq r_\mathbf{x}\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
Part (iii) establishes functoriality only for the extension-degree factor \(r_\mathbf{x}\). It does not automatically imply functoriality of the full height \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}\), because the inner min-max term may behave differently under a general morphism \(\phi\).
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
(i) By definition,
\[
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})=r_\mathbf{x}\cdot\min_{\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times}\max_i\frac{\deg(\lambda^{w_i}x_i)}{w_i}.
\]
The inner min-max term is always at least \(1/\min_i w_i>0\) (since \(\deg(\cdot)\geq1\)). Therefore \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})\leq B\) forces
\[
r_\mathbf{x}\leq B\cdot\min_i w_i.
\]
There are only finitely many positive integers \(r\leq B\cdot\min_i w_i\). For each such \(r\), every geometric point \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(r_\mathbf{x}=r\) admits a representative defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}\), hence determines an \(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}\)-rational point of \(X\).
Since each \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\) is finite, only finitely many geometric points can occur. Therefore the total set of geometric points of bounded height is finite.

(ii) Let \(\mathbf{x}'=\mu\cdot\mathbf{x}\) for some \(\mu\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\). Then any representative of \(\mathbf{x}'\) is of the form \((\mu^{w_i}x_i)\). The weighted orbit of \(\mathbf{x}'\) consists of points
\[
\lambda^{w_i}(\mu^{w_i}x_i)=(\lambda\mu)^{w_i}x_i,
\]
so as \(\lambda\) runs through \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\), the set \(\{\lambda\mu\mid\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\}\) is again the full group \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\). Therefore the minimum taken over the orbit of \(\mathbf{x}'\) is identical to the minimum taken over the orbit of \(\mathbf{x}\). Hence \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}')=H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})\).

(iii) Suppose \(\phi\) is given by polynomials with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}_q\). Let \(\mathbf{x}\) be a geometric point with minimal field of definition \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r_\mathbf{x}}}\), i.e., \(\mathbf{x}\) admits a representative with coordinates in \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r_\mathbf{x}}}\). Since the defining equations of \(\phi\) have coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}_q\), applying \(\phi\) to this representative yields a representative of \(\phi(\mathbf{x})\) whose coordinates also lie in \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r_\mathbf{x}}}\). Therefore the minimal extension degree of \(\phi(\mathbf{x})\) satisfies \(r_{\phi(\mathbf{x})}\leq r_\mathbf{x}\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
The stronger coordinate-degree subadditivity
\[
\deg(f_j(x))\leq d_j \max_i\deg(x_i)
\]
does not hold in general over finite fields, so we state only the safe functoriality of the extension degree \(r_\mathbf{x}\).
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:deg-status}
We call \(H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}\) a height because it satisfies the Northcott property and is formally modelled on the weighted height of \cite{b-g-sh}, with extension degrees in place of valuations. It should be understood, however, as a complexity statistic attached to the chosen weighted coordinates, not as an intrinsic Weil height.  We prove invariance under the weighted \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-action and the common reduction of the weights, but we do not claim invariance under arbitrary automorphisms of the weighted projective space, nor do we attach a line-bundle interpretation to it.  The intrinsic quantity entering its definition is \(r_\mathbf{x}\), the degree of the residue field of the coarse point. None of the main results of \cref{sec:9} depends on \(H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}\).
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{COR1}
Let \(d=\gcd(\mathbf{w})\) and let \(\mathbf{w}'=\mathbf{w}/d\). Let \(\mathbf{x}\in X\subset\mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbf{w}}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\in X'\subset\mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbf{w}'}\) be corresponding points on the isomorphic hypersurfaces (with the reduced weight vector \(\mathbf{w}'\)). Then
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}')=d\cdot H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}).
\]
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Since \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\) are represented by the same homogeneous coordinates, their minimal fields of definition coincide, so \(r_{\mathbf{x}'}=r_\mathbf{x}\). Therefore,
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}')=r_\mathbf{x}\cdot\min_{\mu\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times}\max_i\frac{\deg(\mu^{w_i/d}x_i)}{w_i/d}.
\]
Perform the change of variables \(\mu=\lambda^d\) with \(\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\). Then
\[
\mu^{w_i/d}=(\lambda^d)^{w_i/d}=\lambda^{w_i},
\]
so
\[
\deg(\mu^{w_i/d}x_i)=\deg(\lambda^{w_i}x_i).
\]
Hence
\[
\max_i\frac{\deg(\mu^{w_i/d}x_i)}{w_i/d}=d\cdot\max_i\frac{\deg(\lambda^{w_i}x_i)}{w_i}.
\]
It remains to check that the substitution \(\mu=\lambda^d\) runs over the entire group \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\) as \(\lambda\) does. Since \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q\) is algebraically closed, the map
\[
\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times,\qquad\lambda\mapsto\lambda^d
\]
is surjective. Therefore the set of values attained by the min-max expression for the primed weights is exactly \(d\) times the corresponding expression for the original weights.

Multiplying by the common factor \(r_\mathbf{x}\) yields
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}')=d\cdot H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}).
\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:deg-bounds}
For any geometric point \(\mathbf{x} \in X(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)\),
\[
\frac{r_\mathbf{x}}{\min_i w_i} \;\leq\; H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}) \;\leq\; \frac{r_\mathbf{x}^{2}}{\min_i w_i}.
\]
In particular \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x})=1/\min_i w_i\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q})\).
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For any fixed \(\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^\times\), each coordinate satisfies \(\deg(\lambda^{w_i}x_i)\geq 1\) (adopting the convention \(\deg(0)=1\)). Hence
\[
\max_i \frac{\deg(\lambda^{w_i}x_i)}{w_i} \geq \max_i\frac{1}{w_i} = \frac{1}{\min_i w_i}.
\]
The minimum over \(\lambda\) is still bounded below by the same quantity. Multiplying by \(r_\mathbf{x}\) yields the lower bound. For the upper bound take \(\lambda=1\) and a representative with coordinates in \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r_\mathbf{x}}}\); then \(\deg(x_i)\leq r_\mathbf{x}\) for all \(i\), so the inner term is at most \(r_\mathbf{x}/\min_i w_i\). If \(r_\mathbf{x}=1\) the two bounds agree.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
Let \(X_K = X\times_{\mathbb{F}_{q}} K\) be the base change of \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}}^n\) to \(K = \mathbb{F}_q(t)\).
Let \(\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K)\) be a \(K\)-point of the coarse variety. By \cref{lem:lifting} applied to \(k=K\), it has a weighted-homogeneous representative \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\tilde{x}_0 , \dots , \tilde{x}_n)\) in \(K^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\). The \textbf{function field weighted height} of \(\mathbf{x}\) is
 
\begin{equation}\label{height-FF}
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{v \in M_K} \max_{0\le i\le n} \, \frac{\log |\tilde{x}_i|_v}{w_i},
\end{equation}
where \(v\) runs over all places of \(K\). For a finite extension \(L/K\) and \(\mathbf{x}\in X_K(L)\) the height is defined by the same formula, with \(v\) running over the places of \(L\) and \(|a|_v=|\kappa(v)|^{-\operatorname{ord}_v(a)}\) for the residue field \(\kappa(v)\) at \(v\); this is the absolute normalization, in which \(H^{\mathrm{FF}}\) scales by \([L:K]\) under base change and not by \(1\).
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
For any point \(\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K)\), the function field weighted height \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\) is well-defined and independent of the choice of weighted-homogeneous representative \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} \in K^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\). Moreover \(m\, H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\) is the logarithmic Weil height of \(\phi_m(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{P}^n(K)\), where \(m=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathbf{w})\); in particular \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}\) takes values in \(\frac{\log q}{m}\,\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\).
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
At each place \(v\) one has
\[
\max_i \frac{\log|\tilde x_i|_v}{w_i} = \frac1m \max_i \log\bigl|\tilde x_i^{\,m/w_i}\bigr|_v ,
\]
so \(m\,H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\) is the Weil height of the vector \(\phi_m(\tilde\mathbf{x})\). If \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\) is a second representative in \(K^{n+1}\), then \(\tilde{y}_i = f^{w_i} \tilde{x}_i\) for some \(f \in \bar K^\times\) with \(f^{w_i}\in K\) for all \(i\) in the support, hence \(f^{m}\in K^\times\) and \(\phi_m(\tilde\mathbf{y})=f^m\phi_m(\tilde\mathbf{x})\). By the product formula
\[
\sum_{v \in M_K} \log |f^m|_v = 0
\]
the two vectors have the same height, which is the height of the point \(\phi_m(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{P}^n(K)\). The Weil height on \(\mathbb{P}^n(K)\) is a non-negative integer multiple of \(\log q\).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:FF-finiteness}
Let $X $ be a weighted hypersurface in $\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}}^n$ over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) and \(K=\mathbb{F}_q(t)\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For any  constant \(B>0\), the set
\(
\{\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K) \mid H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x}) \leq B\}
\)
is finite.
\item \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0\), with equality if and only if \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q})\subset X_K(K)\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
(i) The Veronese map \(\phi_m\colon \mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w}\to\mathbb{P}^n\) is finite, and \(h(\phi_m(\mathbf{x})) = m\,H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\) by the lemma. By the Northcott property for \(\mathbb{P}^n\) over the global function field \(K\), whose constant field is finite, there are finitely many points of \(\mathbb{P}^n(K)\) of height at most \(mB\); each has finitely many preimages.

(ii) Non-negativity is that of the Weil height. If \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})=0\), then \(\phi_m(\mathbf{x})\) is a point of height zero in \(\mathbb{P}^n(K)\), that is, a point of \(\mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{F}_{q})\). Its fibre \(Z\) under \(\phi_m\) is a finite \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\)-scheme, and \(Z(K)=Z(\mathbb{F}_{q})\) since \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) is algebraically closed in \(K\). Conversely a point with coordinates in \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) has \(|\tilde x_i|_v\in\{0,1\}\) for all \(v\).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
See e.g.\ Bombieri--Gubler \cite{h-silv} \S2.4 for the Northcott property over function fields. Applied over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}(t)\), part (ii) says that the \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\)-points of \(X\) are precisely the points of function-field height zero. Thus \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}\) detects nonconstant points over the function field.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{PP2}
Let \(\phi: X \to Y\) be a morphism of weighted varieties defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), induced by
\[
\phi([x_0:\dots:x_n]) = [f_0(x):\dots:f_m(x)],
\]
where each \(f_j\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x_0,\dots,x_n]\) is weighted homogeneous of degree \(e w'_j\) for a common integer \(e\), with target \(Y\subset \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}^m\). Then for every \(\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K)\),
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\phi(\mathbf{x})) \leq e \cdot H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x}),
\]
with equality if the \(f_j\) have no common zero on \(\hat X\setminus\{0\}\).
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Put \(M_v=\max_i|\tilde x_i|_v^{1/w_i}\). A monomial \(\prod x_i^{a_i}\) of weighted degree \(\sum a_iw_i = ew'_j\) satisfies \(\prod|\tilde x_i|_v^{a_i}\le M_v^{\,ew'_j}\). The coefficients of \(f_j\) lie in \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) and have absolute value at most \(1\) at every place, so the ultrametric inequality gives \(|f_j(\tilde\mathbf{x})|_v^{1/w'_j}\le M_v^{\,e}\) for all \(v\) and \(j\). Taking logarithms and summing over \(v\) gives the upper bound. For the reverse inequality, if the \(f_j\) have no common zero on \(\hat X\setminus\{0\}\), the homogeneous Nullstellensatz in the graded coordinate ring of \(\hat X\) gives, for each \(i\), an integer \(N_i\) and weighted-homogeneous \(g_{ij}\) of degree \(w_iN_i-ew'_j\) such that \(x_i^{N_i}=\sum_j g_{ij}f_j\) on \(\hat X\). Put \(M'_v=\max_j|f_j(\tilde\mathbf{x})|_v^{1/w'_j}\) and choose \(i\) with \(|\tilde x_i|_v^{1/w_i}=M_v\). Then
\[
M_v^{\,w_iN_i} \le \max_j M_v^{\,w_iN_i-ew'_j}\,(M'_v)^{w'_j},
\]
so \(M_v^{\,e}\le M'_v\). No constant appears because all coefficients are constants of \(K\).
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{COR2}
Let \(\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K)\) and \(\mathbf{x}' \in X'_K(K)\) be corresponding points on isomorphic hypersurfaces under the reduction \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}/d\). Then
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x}') = d \cdot H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x}).
\]
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The two points have the same representatives, and at every place \[\frac{\log|\tilde x_i|_v}{w_i/d} = d\cdot\frac{\log|\tilde x_i|_v}{w_i}.\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
For a point \(\mathbf{x} \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\) with representative \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\in\hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\{0\}\), the \textbf{probabilistic weighted height} is
\[
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x})
=
-\log\left(
\frac{|\operatorname{Orb}_{\mathbf{w}}(\tilde\mathbf{x})|}{|\hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\setminus\{0\}|}
\right),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Orb}_{\mathbf{w}}(\tilde\mathbf{x})\) denotes the orbit of \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\) under the weighted action of
\(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}^{\times}\), namely
\[
\operatorname{Orb}_{\mathbf{w}}(\tilde\mathbf{x})
=
\left\{
(\lambda^{w_0}x_0,\dots,\lambda^{w_n}x_n)
\;\middle|\;
\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^r}^{\times}
\right\}\subset \hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\{0\}.
\]
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:prob-formula}
The function \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}\) is independent of the choice of representative, and
\[
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}) = \log |X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| + \log g_{\mathbf{x}}(r),
\qquad g_\mathbf{x}(r)=\gcd(k_{S(\mathbf{x})},q^r-1).
\]
In particular
\[
\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| \;\le\; H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}) \;\le\; \log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| + \log\max_i w_i ,
\]
with equality on the left if and only if \(\mathbf{x}\) has a single twist over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\).
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:twists}, every orbit of a representative of \(\mathbf{x}\) has \((q^r-1)/g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) elements and the cone has \((q^r-1)|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\) nonzero points. The quotient is \(1/(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\,|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|)\), which depends only on the support of \(\mathbf{x}\). The bounds follow from \(1\le g_\mathbf{x}(r)\le k_{S(\mathbf{x})}\le\max_iw_i\).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{ppp3}
Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n\) and \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}^m\) be weighted hypersurfaces defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and let \(\phi: X \to Y\) be a morphism of weighted varieties as in \cref{PP2}. For any point \(\mathbf{x} \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\),
\[
H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\text{Prob}}(\phi(\mathbf{x})) - H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}) = \log \left( \frac{|Y(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})|}{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})|} \right) + \log \left( \frac{g_{\phi(\mathbf{x})}(r)}{g_{\mathbf{x}}(r)} \right).
\]
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Subtract the two expressions given by \cref{prop:prob-formula}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{COR3}
Let \(X \subset \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n\) and \(X' \subset \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}^n\) be the isomorphic hypersurfaces with weights related by \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}/d\). For any point \(\mathbf{x} \in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\) with corresponding point \(\mathbf{x}'\) in \(X'\) and support \(S\), we have
\[
H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}) - H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}') = \log \left( \frac{\gcd(k_S, q^r - 1)}{\gcd(k_S/d, q^r - 1)} \right),
\]
which lies between \(0\) and \(\log\gcd(d,q^r-1)\), and equals \(\log\gcd(d,q^r-1)\) whenever \(\gcd(d,k_S/d)=1\).
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The coarse varieties coincide, so \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|=|X'(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\), and the stabilizers are \(\mu_{k_S}\) and \(\mu_{k_S/d}\). For the quotient of the two gcd's, put \(N=q^r-1\), which is prime to \(p\). For a prime \(\ell\) write \(a=v_\ell(k_S)\), \(e=v_\ell(d)\), \(n=v_\ell(N)\); then
\[
v_\ell\Bigl(\frac{\gcd(k_S,N)}{\gcd(k_S/d,N)}\Bigr)=\min(a,n)-\min(a-e,n)\in[0,\min(e,n)],
\]
so the quotient is an integer dividing \(\gcd(d,N)\), in any characteristic. When \(p\nmid d\) this is the index computed cohomologically in \cite[Cor.~4.3]{paper-1}. Finally \(\gcd(ab,N)=\gcd(a,N)\gcd(b,N)\) when \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), which gives equality when \(\gcd(d,k_S/d)=1\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- exa-1: body_md -->
\label{exa:running}
Let \(\mathbf{w}=(1,1,2)\) and \(X=\{x_0=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^2\), so that \(X\cong\mathbb{P}(1,2)\) with coordinates \([x_1:x_2]\) and coarse space \(\mathbb{P}^1\). Then \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|=q^r+1\). The point \([0:0:1]\) has stabilizer \(\mu_2\), all other points have trivial stabilizer, and \(g_{[0:0:1]}(r)=\gcd(2,q^r-1)\). For \(q\) odd there are two twists over \([0:0:1]\), and \(q^r+2\) twists in all.
<!-- end exa-1 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:entropy-bound}
	For every weighted hypersurface
\(
X\subset \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}}^{n}
\)
with \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})\neq \varnothing\),
\[
0
\leq
\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\deg}(X)
\leq
\log |\operatorname{Supp}(\mu_{q^r}^{\deg})|.
\]
Moreover,
\[
|\operatorname{Supp}(\mu_{q^r}^{\deg})|
\leq
\sigma(r)\,\frac{w_0+\cdots+w_n}{\min_i w_i},
\]
where \(\sigma(r)\) is the sum of the divisors of \(r\), and \(\operatorname{Ent}_{q}^{\deg}(X)=0\).
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The first inequality is the standard entropy bound for a probability measure
	on a finite set.

	It therefore suffices to estimate the number of possible values of
	\(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}\) on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).  For such a point \(r_{\mathbf{x}}\mid r\). The inner min-max term is attained at some \(\lambda\) and some index \(j\), so it has the form \(k/w_j\) with \(k\) a positive integer, and by \cref{prop:deg-bounds} it is at most \(r_\mathbf{x}/\min_iw_i\). Hence \(k\le r_\mathbf{x} w_j/\min_i w_i\), and for fixed \(r_\mathbf{x}\) and \(j\) there are at most \(r_\mathbf{x} w_j/\min_iw_i\) values. Summing over \(j\) and over the divisors \(r_\mathbf{x}\) of \(r\) gives the bound. For \(r=1\) the height is constant on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q})\) by \cref{prop:deg-bounds}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- exa-2: body_md -->
For the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running} and \( r = 1 \), every \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q})\) has \( H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}(\mathbf{x}) = 1 \), so \(\mathcal{H}_1^{\deg}(X, \mathbb{F}_q) = X(\mathbb{F}_q)\) and \(\mu_q^{\deg}(1) = 1\), yielding \(\operatorname{Ent}_q^{\deg}(X) = 0\). For \( r = 2 \), a point \([0:1:x_2]\) with \( x_2 \in \mathbb{F}_{q^2} \setminus \mathbb{F}_q \) has \(r_\mathbf{x}=2\) and inner term \(\max(1,1,2/2)=1\), hence height \(2\). Thus
\[
\mu_{q^2}^{\deg}(1)=\frac{q+1}{q^2+1},\qquad \mu_{q^2}^{\deg}(2)=\frac{q^2-q}{q^2+1},
\]
which diversifies \(\mu_{q^2}^{\deg}\).
<!-- end exa-2 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:escape}
Let \( X \) be geometrically irreducible of dimension \(n-1\ge1\). Then \(\mu^{\deg}(m)=0\) for every \(m\). More precisely, for every \(M>0\),
\[
\frac{\#\{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}) : H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\le M\}}{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|} = O\bigl(q^{-r(n-1)}\bigr).
\]
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:deg-bounds}, the inequality \(H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\le M\) forces \(r_\mathbf{x}\le M\min_iw_i\). Thus the numerator is bounded by \(\sum_{e\le M\min_i w_i}|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^e})|\), independently of \(r\). The denominator is \(q^{r(n-1)}(1+o(1))\) by Lang--Weil \cite{lang-weil}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
The points of \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) with \(r_\mathbf{x}<r\) number \(O(q^{r(n-1)/2})\), so almost all points are primitive, and for these \cref{prop:deg-bounds} gives \(r/\min_i w_i\le H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\le r^2/\min_iw_i\). The natural object as \(r\to\infty\) is therefore the distribution of the normalized height \(H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}/r^2\) on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), supported in \((0,1/\min_iw_i]\).
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:ff-geometric}
Suppose \(N^{\mathrm{FF}}(k)=c\,\rho^{k}(1+o(1))\) as \(k\to\infty\), for some \(c>0\) and \(\rho>1\). Then the distribution of \(B-k\) under \(\mu^{\mathrm{FF}}_B\) converges to the geometric distribution \(j\mapsto(1-\rho^{-1})\rho^{-j}\), and
\[
\lim_{B\to\infty}\operatorname{Ent}^{\mathrm{FF}}_B(X) = -\log\bigl(1-\rho^{-1}\bigr)+\frac{\log\rho}{\rho-1}.
\]
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The denominator is \(c\rho^{B}(1-\rho^{-1})^{-1}(1+o(1))\), so \(\mu_B^{\mathrm{FF}}(B-j)\to(1-\rho^{-1})\rho^{-j}\) for each fixed \(j\). Moreover \(\mu^{\mathrm{FF}}_B(B-j)\le C\rho^{-j}\) uniformly in \(B\), and \(-x\log x\) is increasing near \(0\), so the terms of the entropy sum are dominated by a summable sequence and the entropy converges to that of the limit. For \(p_j=(1-\tau)\tau^{j}\) with \(\tau=\rho^{-1}\) one computes \(-\sum_jp_j\log p_j=-\log(1-\tau)-\frac{\tau}{1-\tau}\log\tau\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- exa-3: body_md -->
\label{exa:P1}
Let \(\mathbf{w}=(1,1,1)\) and \(X=\{x_0=0\}\cong\mathbb{P}^1\). A point of \(X_K(K)\) of height \(k\log q\) is a morphism \(\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1\) of degree \(k\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), so \(N^{\mathrm{FF}}(0)=q+1\) and \(N^{\mathrm{FF}}(k)=q^{2k+1}-q^{2k-1}\) for \(k\ge1\). Here \(\rho=q^2\), and
\(
\lim_B\operatorname{Ent}^{\mathrm{FF}}_B(X) = -\log(1-q^{-2})+\frac{2\log q}{q^2-1}.
\)
<!-- end exa-3 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:phillips}
Two counting problems over \(K\) must be kept apart. In \cite{Phillips2024} the objects of \(\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}(K)\), that is the \(K^\times\)-orbits, are counted by the height with ceilings, which is \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}\) of \cref{sec:6}. The strata \(\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{FF}}_k\) above consist instead of coarse points ordered by the stable height; by \cref{prop:ff-spec} this is the Weil height of the image under \(\phi_m\), divided by \(m\).  These are different counting problems.  In the running example the coarse space is \(\mathbb{P}^1\), and the explicit formula of \cref{exa:P1} applies.  More generally, if several dominant poles occur on the circle \(|u|=\rho^{-1}\), the coefficient asymptotics can acquire a periodic factor, as noted after \cref{prop:entropy-pole}; no single-term asymptotic is asserted here without the hypothesis of \cref{prop:ff-geometric}.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
If \(\gcd(w_i,q^r-1)=1\) for all \(i\), then every \(g_S(r)=1\), there is a single stratum, and \(\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\text{Prob}}(X)=0\). The entropy \(\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\text{Prob}}(X)\) measures isotropy diversity; it is nonzero only in the presence of the Kummer twists of \cite{paper-1}, which are the finite-field counterpart of the gcd-obstructions in \cite{sh-94}.
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- exa-4: body_md -->
\label{exa:prob}
For the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running} and \(q\) odd there are two strata, the point \([0:0:1]\) and its complement, so
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X) = \log(q^r+1)-\frac{q^r}{q^r+1}\log q^r ,
\]
which is asymptotic to \(r\log q\cdot q^{-r}\). For \(q\) even the entropy vanishes for all \(r\).
<!-- end exa-4 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduction-entropy}
Let $X \subset \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n$ and $X' \subset \mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}^n$ be the isomorphic hypersurfaces under the reduction $\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}/d$.
 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\deg}(X) = \operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\deg}(X')$ for all \(r\).
\item $\operatorname{Ent}_{B}^{\mathrm{FF}}(X) = \operatorname{Ent}_{B}^{\mathrm{FF}}(X')$ for all \(B\).
\item $\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\text{Prob}}(X) \le \operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\text{Prob}}(X')$, with equality if \(\gcd(d,q^r-1)=1\), and the inequality can be strict.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
i) The point sets \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) and \(X'(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) coincide, and by \cref{COR1} the stratum $\mathcal{H}_m^{\deg}(X,\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})$ is the stratum $\mathcal{H}_{d \cdot m}^{\deg}(X',\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})$. The two profiles differ by the relabeling \(m\mapsto dm\), which does not change the entropy.

ii) By \cref{COR2} the same argument applies; note that \(\operatorname{lcm}(\mathbf{w}')=\operatorname{lcm}(\mathbf{w})/d\), so the index \(k\) of a stratum is unchanged.

iii) If \(\gcd(d,q^r-1)=1\), then \(\gcd(k_S,q^r-1)=\gcd(k_S/d,q^r-1)\) for every \(S\) and the isotropy strata coincide. In general the relationship between $H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x})$ and $H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\text{Prob}}(\mathbf{x}')$ is point-dependent by \cref{COR3}. We claim that the isotropy stratification for \(\mathbf{w}\) is coarser than that for \(\mathbf{w}'\). Let \(N=q^r-1\) and let \(k_1',k_2'\) be two values of \(k_S/d\) with \(\gcd(k'_1,N)=\gcd(k'_2,N)\). For each prime \(\ell\), either \(v_\ell(k_1')=v_\ell(k'_2)\) or both are at least \(v_\ell(N)\); in either case \(\min(v_\ell(dk'_1),v_\ell(N))=\min(v_\ell(dk'_2),v_\ell(N))\), so \(\gcd(dk_1',N)=\gcd(dk'_2,N)\). Merging strata does not increase the entropy, which gives the inequality. For example, take \(X'\) as in \cref{exa:running} and \(\mathbf{w}=(2,2,4)\), with \(q^r\equiv 3\pmod 4\). For \(\mathbf{w}'\) the point \([0:0:1]\) has \(g=2\) and all others have \(g=1\), so \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X')>0\) by \cref{exa:prob}. For \(\mathbf{w}\) the point \([0:0:1]\) has \(g=\gcd(4,q^r-1)=2\) and all others have \(g=\gcd(2,q^r-1)=2\), so there is a single stratum and \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=0\). When \(q^r\equiv1\pmod 4\) the two entropies agree.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:prob-asymptotics}
Let \(X \subset \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n\) be a geometrically irreducible weighted hypersurface over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) of dimension \(n-1\ge1\), and let \(r\) satisfy \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\ne\varnothing\).  Let \(\kappa_r\) be the number of distinct values among the \(g_S(r)\) occurring on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).  Whenever \(\varepsilon_r\le 1/2\),
\[
h(\varepsilon_r)\le \operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)
\le h(\varepsilon_r)+\varepsilon_r\log(\kappa_r-1)
\]
when \(\kappa_r\ge2\); if \(\kappa_r=1\), then \(\varepsilon_r=0\) and \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=0\).

Uniformly in \(r\), one has \(\varepsilon_r=O(q^{-r})\) and hence
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=O(rq^{-r}).
\]
More precisely, if \(\Sigma_r\neq\varnothing\) and \(N_r\ge1\), then along each residue class modulo \(M\),
\[
\varepsilon_r=N_rq^{-rc_r}\bigl(1+O(q^{-r/2})\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)
=c_rN_r\,r\log q\,q^{-rc_r}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr).
\]
The implied constants can be chosen uniformly over the finitely many residue classes modulo \(M\).
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
If \(\kappa_r=1\), there is a single isotropy stratum and the entropy is zero.  Assume \(\kappa_r\ge2\).  The stratum \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\Sigma_r(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) has mass \(1-\varepsilon_r\).  By the grouping property of Shannon entropy,
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=h(\varepsilon_r)+\varepsilon_r E_r,
\]
where \(E_r\) is the entropy of the conditional distribution on the remaining at most \(\kappa_r-1\) strata.  Hence \(0\le E_r\le\log(\kappa_r-1)\), proving the first assertion.

Only finitely many closed subschemes \(\Sigma_r\) occur as \(r\) varies modulo \(M_{\rm iso}\).  Since each is a proper closed subset of \(X\), Lang--Weil gives the uniform bound \(|\Sigma_r(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|=O(q^{r(\dim X-1)})\), while \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|=q^{r\dim X}(1+O(q^{-r/2}))\).  Thus \(\varepsilon_r=O(q^{-r})\), and the entropy bound follows from \(h(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))\).

Fix now a residue class modulo \(M\) for which \(\Sigma_r\neq\varnothing\) and \(N_r\ge1\).  On that class the closed set \(\Sigma_r\), its codimension \(c_r\), and the number \(N_r\) of Frobenius-stable top-dimensional geometric components are constant.  Lang--Weil, applied to those components and to their lower-dimensional intersections, gives
\[
|\Sigma_r(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|=N_rq^{r(\dim X-c_r)}+O\bigl(q^{r(\dim X-c_r-1/2)}\bigr).
\]
Dividing by the Lang--Weil estimate for \(X\) gives the asserted formula for \(\varepsilon_r\).  Finally,
\(h(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)+O(\varepsilon)\), while the conditional-entropy term is \(O(\varepsilon_r)\); this yields the stated leading term for \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)\).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
The period in \cref{thm:prob-asymptotics} has two sources.  The closed set \(\Sigma_r\) is controlled by the periodic isotropy functions \(g_S(r)\), whereas \(N_r\) is controlled by the Frobenius action on the geometric components of that closed set.  These periods need not coincide: \cref{exa:fe-diag} has constant order-two isotropy over odd fields, while its two geometric exceptional points are rational only over extensions in which \(-1\) becomes a square.  The leading entropy term is therefore a Lang--Weil term on arithmetic subsequences, not a function of the isotropy period alone.
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:char}
We separate three kinds of statements. (a) All statements about the groupoids \(\mathfrak X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\)---twists, rational automorphisms, mass, the heights \(H^{\text{Prob}}\) and \(H^{\operatorname{stack}}\), the entropies, the loci \(X^\zeta\) and \(\Sigma_r\), and the zeta function \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H\)---are statements about point counts of the tame Artin stack \(\mathfrak X\) and hold in every characteristic; only the prime-to-\(p\) part of \(k_S\) enters, since \(\gcd(k_S,q^r-1)\) is prime to \(p\). (b) The identification of the loci \(X^\zeta\) with the components of the inertia stack, the comparison of the cohomology of \(\mathfrak X\) and \(X\), and the word ``twisted sector'' in its usual sense, require \(\mathfrak X\) to be a tame Deligne--Mumford stack, that is \(p\nmid w_i\) for all \(i\); when \(p\mid k_S\) the stabilizer \(\mu_{k_S}\) is non-reduced and the inertia stack is not a disjoint union of such loci. (c) Comparisons with Chen--Ruan cohomology, orbifold Euler characteristics and index theorems refer to the characteristic-zero theory and are made by analogy only. When \(p\) divides some weight we still call \(X^\zeta\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times\), a \textbf{rational isotropy locus}, and use ``twisted sector'' only under the hypothesis of (b).
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:mass}
For every \(r\ge1\) and every \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), the twists lying over \(\mathbf{x}\) have total mass \(1\). Consequently the pushforward of the mass measure on \(\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))\) to the coarse space is the counting measure on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), and
\[
\#^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^r})) = |X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| .
\]
The mass of a twist \(\xi\) is \(|\operatorname{Orb}_\mathbf{w}(\tilde\mathbf{x})|/(q^r-1)\), where \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\) is any vector in the orbit \(\xi\).
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:twists} there are \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) twists over \(\mathbf{x}\), each with automorphism group of order \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) and orbit of size \((q^r-1)/g_\mathbf{x}(r)\). For \(X=\mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w}\) this is \cite[Prop.~3.9]{paper-1}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- exa-5: body_md -->
\label{exa:mass}
For the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running}, whose stack is the stacky line \(\mathcal{P}(1,2)\) with a \(\mu_2\)-point, and \(q\) odd: there are \(q\) twists with trivial automorphism group and two twists over \([0:0:1]\), each of mass \(1/2\). Thus the number of twists is \(q+2\), while \(\#^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q})) = q + 1=|X(\mathbb{F}_{q})|\).
<!-- end exa-5 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:stack-height-inv}
Each of \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\operatorname{stack},\deg}\) and \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\operatorname{stack},\mathrm{FF}}\) is invariant under reduction of the weights. That is, if \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w} / d\), then \(H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\operatorname{stack},\bullet}(\mathbf{x}') = H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\operatorname{stack},\bullet}(\mathbf{x})\) for corresponding points \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\).
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Under the reduction \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w} / d\), the stack \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{w}}\) is a \(\mu_d\)-gerbe over \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}\), and a point of support \(S\) has stabilizer \(\mu_{k_S}\) in the first and \(\mu_{k_S/d}\) in the second \cite[Prop.~4.1]{paper-1}. Thus \(|\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{x}')| = |\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{x})|/d\).
The underlying height scales as \(H_{\mathbf{w}',q}(\mathbf{x}')=d\,H_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\) by \cref{COR1} and \cref{COR2}, and the factor \(|\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf{x})|\) compensates exactly, yielding \(H_{\mathbf{w}',q}^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathbf{x}') = H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathbf{x})\).
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:prob-mass}
Let \(p_r\) be the mass measure on \(\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))\) normalized to total mass one. For a twist \(\xi\) lying over \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\),
\[
H^{\text{Prob}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x}) = -\log p_r(\xi) = \log\#^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})) + \log|\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| .
\]
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:mass}, \(p_r(\xi)=|\operatorname{Orb}_\mathbf{w}(\tilde\mathbf{x})|/|\hat X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\setminus\{0\}|\), and the second equality is \cref{prop:prob-formula}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:stack-entropy-inv}
Let \(\mathfrak{X} \subset \mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}\) and \(\mathfrak{X}' \subset \mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}\) be the stacks of the same hypersurface, with \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}/d\). Then:
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}) = \operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}').
\]
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:mass} the mass of \(\mathcal{H}_m^{\operatorname{stack}}\) is the number of \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) with \(H^{\operatorname{stack}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})=m\), for \(\mathfrak X\) and for \(\mathfrak X'\) alike. The coarse point sets coincide and the stacky heights agree by \cref{prop:stack-height-inv}, so the strata have the same masses,
\[
\#^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathcal{H}_m^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}, \mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})) = \#^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathcal{H}_m^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}', \mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})),
\]
and similarly for the total mass, yielding identical \(\mu^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r}(m)\) and hence equal entropies.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:stack-zeta}
For a weighted hypersurface \(\mathfrak{X} \subset \mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) with coarse space \(X\),
\[
Z^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}, t) = Z(X,t).
\]
In particular \(Z^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X}, t)\) is rational and unchanged under reduction of the weights. Each reciprocal zero or pole is a Frobenius eigenvalue on some \(H^i_c(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q},\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\), hence a \(q\)-Weil integer of some integer weight \(j\) with \(0\le j\le i\le 2(n-1)\): an algebraic integer all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value \(q^{j/2}\). Since \(X\) may be singular the cohomology is mixed, and \(j<i\) can occur.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The equality is \cref{prop:mass}. The coarse space \(X\) is a projective variety over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), so \(Z(X,t)\) is rational by Dwork's theorem \cite{dwork1960}, by the Grothendieck--Lefschetz trace formula its reciprocal zeros and poles are Frobenius eigenvalues on the groups \(H^i_c(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q},\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\), and by Deligne's theorem \cite{deligne-weil2} each eigenvalue on \(H^i_c\) is an algebraic integer which is pure of some integer weight \(j\le i\). The coarse varieties of \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\mathbf{w}/d\) coincide.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- rem-11: body_md -->
When \(p\nmid w_i\) for all \(i\), the mass identity can also be read cohomologically from the trace formula for tame Deligne--Mumford stacks \cite{Behrend}.  The twist zeta function is different: it counts isomorphism classes without inverse-automorphism weights.  Its functional equation is treated in \cref{subsec:fe}.
<!-- end rem-11 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
The stacky entropy satisfies \(0 \leq \operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}) \leq \log |\operatorname{Supp}(\mu^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r})|\), with equality on the left for a single stratum and on the right for the uniform profile.
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
This is the standard entropy bound for a probability distribution on a finite set. Equality on the right occurs precisely for the uniform distribution on its support.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:inertia}
The isotropy stratification of \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), the profile \(\mu^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}\), and the entropy \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)\) are determined by the numbers \(|X^{\zeta}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times\), together with the inclusions among the \(X^\zeta\). Moreover
\[
\#\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})) = \sum_{\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times}|X^{\zeta}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|,
\qquad
\Sigma_r = \bigcup_{\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times,\ \zeta^{d_X}\neq1} X^{\zeta},
\]
where \(\Sigma_r\) is the locus of \cref{thm:prob-asymptotics}.
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
For \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) the set \(\{\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times : \mathbf{x}\in X^\zeta\}\) is \(\mu_{k_{S(\mathbf{x})}}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), of order \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\). Hence \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) is recovered from the \(X^\zeta\) containing \(\mathbf{x}\), and the number of points with a given isotropy is obtained from the \(|X^\zeta(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\) by inclusion--exclusion. Summing \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) over \(\mathbf{x}\) gives the first formula by \cref{lem:twists}; this is the Burnside form of the orbit count \cite[Lem.~3.1]{paper-1}. Finally \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\neq\gcd(d_X,q^r-1)\) if and only if \(\mu_{k_{S(\mathbf{x})}}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) contains an element outside \(\mu_{d_X}\).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- exa-6: body_md -->
For \(\mathcal{P}(1,2)\) and odd \(q\), the inertia stack is \(\mathcal{P}(1,2)\sqcup B\mu_2\), with the second component over the stacky point and corresponding to \(\zeta=-1\). Accordingly
\[
|X^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})|+|X^{-1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})|=(q+1)+1=q+2,
\]
which is the number of twists, and \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q}=h(1/(q+1))\) as in \cref{exa:prob}.
<!-- end exa-6 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
The \textbf{groupoid entropy}, or canonical entropy, of the groupoid \(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) is the Shannon entropy of the normalized mass measure \(p_r\) on the set of twists,
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}) := -\sum_{\xi\in\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))} p_r(\xi)\log p_r(\xi).
\]
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:gerbe-entropy}
Let \(\mathfrak{X}\) be the stack of \(X \subset \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}) = \log |X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})| + \frac{1}{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})}\log g_\mathbf{x}(r),
\]
the mean of the probabilistic height. If \(\mathbf{w}'=\mathbf{w}/d\) and \(\mathfrak{X}'\subset\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}\), then
\[
0\;\le\;\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X})-\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X}')\;\le\;\log \gcd(d, q^r-1),
\]
with equality on the right when \(\gcd(d,k_S/d)=1\) for every support \(S\) occurring on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), where the log term captures the entropy of the \(\mu_d\)-gerbe.
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Over \(\mathbf{x}\) there are \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) twists, each with \(p_r(\xi)=1/(g_\mathbf{x}(r)|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|)\) by \cref{prop:prob-mass}; their contribution to the entropy is \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|^{-1}\bigl(\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|+\log g_\mathbf{x}(r)\bigr)\). The comparison is the average of \cref{COR3} over \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- rem-12: body_md -->
Let \(\nu_r\) be the uniform probability measure on the set of twists and \(A_X(q^r)=\#\pi_0(\mathfrak{X}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))\). The same computation gives the relative entropy
\[
D(\nu_r\,\|\,p_r) = \mathbb{E}_{\nu_r}\bigl[\log|\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\bigr]-\log\frac{A_X(q^r)}{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|},
\]
which vanishes exactly when all points of \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) have the same number of twists. By \cref{thm:prob-asymptotics} the mean in \cref{prop:gerbe-entropy} is \(\log\gcd(d_X,q^r-1)+O(q^{-rc_r})\), so \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak X)-\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\) is asymptotically periodic in \(r\).
<!-- end rem-12 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\label{def:can-height}
For \(x \in \mathfrak{X}_K(K)\) and a vector bundle \(\mathcal{V}\), the \textbf{height} and the \textbf{stable height} of \cite[Def.~2.11, Def.~2.12]{ellenberg} are
\[
H^{\operatorname{can}}_{\mathcal{V}}(x) = -\deg(\pi_* \bar x^* \mathcal{V}^\vee),
\qquad
H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{\mathcal{V}}(x) = -\deg_{\mathcal{C}}(\bar x^* \mathcal{V}^\vee),
\]
where \((\mathcal{C}, \bar x, \pi)\) is a tuning stack for \(x\): \(\mathcal{C}\) is a normal Artin stack with finite diagonal, \(\pi: \mathcal{C} \to C\) is a birational coarse space map, and \(\bar x: \mathcal{C} \to \mathfrak{X}\times C\) extends the given \(x: \operatorname{Spec} K \to \mathfrak{X}_K\).
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:ff-spec}
Let \(x\in\mathfrak{X}_K(K)\) be the orbit of \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\), with coarse point \(\mathbf{x}\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x) = H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\), and \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(m)}(x)=m\,H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\mathrm{FF}}(\mathbf{x})\);
\item \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x) = \sum_{v}\bigl\lceil a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\bigr\rceil\log q_v\);
\item the local discrepancy at \(v\) is \(\delta_{{\mathcal O}(1);v}(x)=\bigl(\lceil a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\rceil-a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\bigr)\log q_v\), which lies in \([0,\log q_v)\) and, when nonzero, is at least \(\frac1m\log q_v\).
\end{enumerate}
The stable height depends only on the coarse point \(\mathbf{x}\); the height \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}\) depends on the twist \(x\).
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Write \(\mathcal{L}={\mathcal O}(1)\). The coordinate \(x_i\) is a section of \(\mathcal{L}^{w_i}\), so the \(n+1\) sections \(s_i=x_i^{m/w_i}\) of \(\mathcal{L}^{m}\) have no common zero on \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\); equivalently the map \({\mathcal O}_{\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}}^{\oplus(n+1)}\to\mathcal{L}^m\) they define is surjective. Hence \(\mathcal{L}^m\) is globally generated by \(s_0,\dots,s_n\) on the whole model \(\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}\times C\), and not merely generically globally generated in the sense of \cite[Sec.~2.4]{ellenberg}; this is the situation of \cite[Sec.~3.3]{ellenberg}. Since \(K\) is a function field, \(C\) has no Archimedean places. Both hypotheses of the second, exact assertion of \cite[Prop.~2.28]{ellenberg} therefore hold, so that proposition applies with no bounded error term \(E(x)\). Choosing the identification of \(x^*\mathcal{L}\) with \(K\) given by \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\), the pullbacks of the \(s_i\) are \(\tilde x_i^{m/w_i}\), and \cite[Prop.~2.28]{ellenberg}, applied to the power \(\mathcal{L}^m\), gives
\[
H^{\operatorname{can}}_{\mathcal{L}}(x)=\sum_v\Bigl\lceil\frac1m\log_{q_v}\max_i\bigl|\tilde x_i^{\,m/w_i}\bigr|_v\Bigr\rceil\log q_v=\sum_v\lceil a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\rceil\log q_v,
\]
which is (ii); this is \cite[(3.5)]{ellenberg} for the weights \(\mathbf{w}\).

The Veronese morphism \(\phi_m\colon\mathcal{P}_\mathbf{w}\to\mathbb{P}^n\) satisfies \(\phi_m^*{\mathcal O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(1)=\mathcal{L}^m\).  Since a bundle pulled back from a scheme has equal height and stable height \cite[Prop.~2.15]{ellenberg}, and stable height is additive in tensor powers,
\[
m H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{\mathcal{L}}(x)
 =H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{\mathcal{L}^m}(x)
 =H^{\operatorname{can}}_{\mathcal{L}^m}(x)
 =h(\phi_m(\mathbf{x})).
\]
By \cref{sec:3}, \(h(\phi_m(\mathbf{x}))=mH^{\mathrm{FF}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\), proving the first identity in (i); the same display gives the second.  Subtracting this stable height from the ceiling formula in (ii) gives
\[
\delta_{\mathcal{L};v}(x)=\bigl(\lceil a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\rceil-a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\bigr)\log q_v.
\]
Since \(a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\in\frac1m\mathbb{Z}\), every nonzero discrepancy is at least \(\frac1m\log q_v\).  Replacing \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\) by the twist \((a^{w_i/k_S}\tilde x_i)\) changes \(a_v\) by \(-\operatorname{ord}_v(a)/k_S\); the sum of the stable local terms is unchanged by the product formula, while the ceiling terms can change.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:kummer-finite}
Let \(L\) be a global function field with finite constant field \(\mathbb{F}\), let \(k\ge1\) and \(B\ge0\). The set of classes \(a\in L^\times/(L^\times)^k\) such that
\[
\sum_{v\,:\,k\,\nmid\,\operatorname{ord}_v(a)}\deg v\;\le\;B
\]
is finite.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Consider the homomorphism \(\partial\colon L^\times/(L^\times)^k\to\operatorname{Div}(L)/k\operatorname{Div}(L)\), \(a\mapsto\operatorname{div}(a)\bmod k\). A class in \(\operatorname{Div}(L)/k\operatorname{Div}(L)\) is a function from the places to \(\mathbb{Z}/k\) with finite support, and the condition says that the support of \(\partial(a)\) has degree at most \(B\). There are finitely many places of degree at most \(B\), hence finitely many such classes. It remains to see that \(\ker\partial\) is finite. If \(\operatorname{div}(a)=kD\), then \(\deg D=0\) and the class of \(D\) lies in \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(L)[k]\), which is finite because \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(L)\) is finite for a finite constant field. If this class is trivial, \(D=\operatorname{div}(b)\) and \(a=ub^k\) with \(u\in\mathbb{F}^\times\), so the class of \(a\) lies in the image of \(\mathbb{F}^\times/(\mathbb{F}^\times)^k\), which is finite. Thus \(\ker\partial\) is an extension of a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(L)[k]\) by a quotient of \(\mathbb{F}^\times/(\mathbb{F}^\times)^k\).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:can-properties}
On \(\mathfrak{X}_K\) the heights of \cref{def:can-height} satisfy:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Finiteness (Northcott Property)}: For \(\mathcal{V}={\mathcal O}(1)\), the set \[ \{ x \in \mathfrak{X}_K(L) \mid H^{\operatorname{can}}_{\mathcal{V}}(x) \leq B \}\] is finite for any finite extension \(L/K\) and \(B > 0\).
\item \textbf{Base change}: Under a separable extension \(L/K\), \(H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{\mathcal{V}}(x_L) = [L:K] \cdot H^{\operatorname{can},st}_{\mathcal{V}}(x)\). The unstable height \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_\mathcal{V}\) does not satisfy such a relation in general.
\item \textbf{Functoriality}: If \(f: \mathfrak{X} \to \mathfrak{Y}\) is a morphism of stacks and \({\mathcal W}\) a vector bundle on \(\mathfrak{Y}\), then \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{f^* {\mathcal W}}(x) = H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal W}}(f \circ x)\).
\item \textbf{Schemes}: If \(\mathcal{V}\) is pulled back from a scheme, then \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_\mathcal{V}=H^{\operatorname{can},st}_\mathcal{V}\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
(ii) is \cite[Prop.~2.14]{ellenberg}, (iii) is \cite[Rem.~2.16]{ellenberg}, and (iv) is \cite[Prop.~2.15]{ellenberg}.

For (i) we work over \(L\), with the places of \(L\), and we let \(q\) denote the order of its constant field; \cref{prop:ff-spec} holds over \(L\) with the same proof. Since \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x)\ge H^{\mathrm{FF}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\), \cref{thm:FF-finiteness} over \(L\) shows that only finitely many coarse points \(\mathbf{x}\) occur. Fix one, of support \(S\), with representative \(\tilde\mathbf{x}\), put \(k=k_S\), and let \(V_0\) be the finite set of places with \(a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})\notin\mathbb{Z}\). By \cref{lem:lifting}(iii) the objects over \(\mathbf{x}\) are the orbits \(x_a\) of the vectors \((a^{w_i/k}\tilde x_i)\), \(a\in L^\times/(L^\times)^k\), and
\[
H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x_a)-H^{\mathrm{FF}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_v\delta_v(a),\qquad
\delta_v(a)=\bigl(\lceil y_v\rceil-y_v\bigr)\log q_v,\quad y_v=a_v(\tilde\mathbf{x})-\frac{\operatorname{ord}_v(a)}{k} .
\]
Since \(k\mid w_i\mid m\) for \(i\in S\), the number \(y_v\) lies in \(\frac1m\mathbb{Z}\), so \(\delta_v(a)\ge\frac1m\log q_v\) whenever \(y_v\) is not an integer. For \(v\notin V_0\) this happens exactly when \(k\nmid\operatorname{ord}_v(a)\). Hence \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x_a)\le B\) implies
\[
\sum_{v\,:\,k\,\nmid\,\operatorname{ord}_v(a)}\deg v\;\le\;\frac{mB}{\log q}+\sum_{v\in V_0}\deg v,
\]
and \cref{lem:kummer-finite} leaves finitely many classes \(a\).
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- rem-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:deg-spec}
The degree-based height \(H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg}\) is not a specialization of \(H^{\operatorname{can}}_\mathcal{V}\); see \cref{rem:deg-status}. A point of \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), viewed as a constant point over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}(t)\), has function-field height zero by \cref{thm:FF-finiteness}. The two functions therefore measure different quantities: \(H^{\mathrm{FF}}\) is a sum of local weighted maxima over the places of \(K\), whereas \(H^{\deg}\) records coordinate extension degrees, with the additional factor \(r_\mathbf{x}\).
<!-- end rem-13 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
The \textbf{function-field height zeta function} of \(X\) over \(K=\mathbb{F}_{q}(t)\) is the power series, indexed by the coarse points,
$$Z_{H^{\mathrm{FF}}}(X_K, s) = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in X_K(K)} e^{-s H^{\mathrm{FF}}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})} = \sum_{k\ge0} N^{\mathrm{FF}}(k)\,u^{k},\qquad u=q^{-s/m},$$
with \(N^{\mathrm{FF}}(k)\) as in \cref{sec:4}. The stacky version \(Z_{H^{\operatorname{can}}}(\mathfrak{X}_K, s)\) is the sum of \(e^{-sH^{\operatorname{can}}_{{\mathcal O}(1)}(x)}/|\operatorname{Aut}(x)(K)|\) over isomorphism classes \(x\in\mathfrak X_K(K)\); each level set is finite by \cref{thm:can-properties}(i). We do not study it here.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- prop-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:entropy-pole}
Assume that $Z_{H^{\mathrm{FF}}}(X_K, s)$, as a function of \(u\), is meromorphic in a disc \(|u|<\rho^{-1}+\eta\) with a single pole there, simple and located at \(u=\rho^{-1}\), \(\rho>1\). Then \(N^{\mathrm{FF}}(k)=c\rho^k(1+o(1))\), the abscissa of convergence is \(s_0=m\log\rho/\log q\), and
\[
\lim_{B\to\infty}\operatorname{Ent}_B^{\mathrm{FF}}(X) = -\log\bigl(1-\rho^{-1}\bigr)+\frac{\log\rho}{\rho-1}.
\]
<!-- end prop-18 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Subtracting the principal part \(c/(1-\rho u)\) leaves a function holomorphic in the larger disc, whose coefficients are \(O((\rho^{-1}+\eta')^{-k})\) for some \(\eta'>0\). The rest is \cref{prop:ff-geometric}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- rem-14: body_md -->
Thus, under the stated single-pole hypothesis, the limiting entropy is determined by the dominant pole. In \cref{exa:P1}, \(Z_{H^{\mathrm{FF}}}=(q+1)+(q-q^{-1})\,q^2u/(1-q^2u)\) is rational with its pole at \(u=q^{-2}\). The coefficients are the cardinalities of the strata $\mathcal{H}_k^{\mathrm{FF}}$. If several poles lie on the circle \(|u|=\rho^{-1}\), the coefficient asymptotics acquire a periodic factor; the normalized profile may then fail to converge and the entropy may be asymptotically periodic in \(B\) rather than convergent.
<!-- end rem-14 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
The \textbf{mass power sum} over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\) is
\[
Z^{\operatorname{can}}(\beta;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})=\sum_{\xi\in\pi_0(\mathfrak X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))}p_r(\xi)^\beta,
\]
where \(\beta\ge0\). For the degree-based height we similarly write
\[
Z^{\deg}(\beta;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})=\sum_m e^{-\beta m}|\mathcal{H}_m^{\deg}(X,\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|.
\]
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:duality}
For the mass power sum \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(\beta;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\),
\[
\operatorname{Ent}_{q^r}^{\operatorname{can}}(\mathfrak{X}) = S(1) = -\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \log  Z^{\operatorname{can}}(\beta; \mathbb{F}_{q^r}) \right|_{\beta=1},
\qquad
S(0):=\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}S(\beta)=\log A_X(q^r),
\]
Thus the groupoid entropy is the mean probabilistic height.  At \(\beta=0\) the escort distribution is uniform on the set of twists, while at \(\beta=1\) it is the mass measure.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Since \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(1;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})=1\) and \(p_{r,1}=p_r\), the displayed entropy formula gives \(S(1)=\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak X)\).  Differentiating \(\log\sum_\xi p_r(\xi)^\beta\) at \(\beta=1\) gives the same identity.  At \(\beta=0\), \(p_{r,0}\) is uniform on the \(A_X(q^r)\) twists.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- exa-7: body_md -->
For the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running} with \(q\) odd, \eqref{eq:partition} gives \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(\beta; \mathbb{F}_q) = (q+1)^{-\beta}\bigl(q+2^{1-\beta}\bigr)\), and
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_q(\mathfrak X)=\log(q+1)+\frac{\log 2}{q+1},\qquad S(0)=\log(q+2).
\]
For the weights \((2,2,4)\) and \(q\equiv1\pmod4\) one finds \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_q=\log(q+1)+\frac{q\log2+\log4}{q+1}\), which exceeds the previous value by exactly \(\log 2=\log\gcd(d,q-1)\).
<!-- end exa-7 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
\label{def:taxonomy}
Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite or countable set with a function \(H\colon\mathcal S\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) having finite level sets, and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure with finite support.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If \(H>0\) on \(\mathcal S\), the \textbf{Dirichlet-type height series} is \(D_H(s)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal S}H(\mathbf{x})^{-s}\).
\item The \textbf{Laplace-type height series} is \[L_H(s)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal S}e^{-sH(\mathbf{x})}.\]
\item The \textbf{profile zeta function} of \(\mu\) is \(\zeta_\mu(s)=\sum_m\mu(m)^s\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
For the degree-based height \( H_{\mathbf{w},q}^{\deg} \) on a hypersurface \(X\subset\mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w}\), the series \( Z_{H^{\deg}}^{\infty}(X, s) \) converges absolutely for
\[
\Re(s) > (n-1)\min_i w_i .
\]
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The number of geometric points with \(r_\mathbf{x}=e\) is at most \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^e})|\le C q^{e(n-1)}\). By \cref{prop:deg-bounds} each such point has \(H^{\deg}_{\mathbf{w},q}(\mathbf{x})\ge e/\min_iw_i\). Hence the series is dominated by \(C\sum_{e\ge1} q^{e(n-1)-\Re(s)\,e/\min_i w_i}\), which converges for \(\Re(s)>(n-1)\min_iw_i\).
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- prop-19: body_md -->
Suppose \( Z(u)=\sum_{k\ge0} N(k)u^k \), \(N(k)\ge0\), is meromorphic in a disc \(|u|<\rho^{-1}+\eta\) whose only pole there is a simple pole at \( u = \rho^{-1} \), \(\rho>1\). Then
\[
\sum_{k \leq T} N(k) \sim \frac{c\,\rho}{\rho-1}\, \rho^{T} \quad \text{as } T \to \infty \text{ through integers},
\]
for some constant \( c > 0 \). In particular, \( \rho \) governs the growth rate of points of bounded height on \( X \).
<!-- end prop-19 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
As in \cref{prop:entropy-pole}, \(N(k)=c\rho^k+O(\rho_1^k)\) for some \(\rho_1<\rho\), and one sums the geometric series. For Dirichlet series with a single pole on the line of convergence the corresponding statement is the Wiener--Ikehara theorem (cf. \cite{korevaar-tauberian}); it does not apply directly here, since \(u=q^{-s/m}\) is periodic in \(s\).
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- exa-8: body_md -->
Let \( X \) be the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running}. Over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) the Dirichlet-type series of the degree-based height is \(Z_{H^{\deg}}(X,s;q)=q+1\), and over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\) it is \((q+1)+(q^2-q)2^{-s}\). The Laplace-type series of the probabilistic height on the twists is \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(s;\mathbb{F}_{q})=(q+1)^{-s}(q+2^{1-s})\) for \(q\) odd.
<!-- end exa-8 -->
<!-- rem-15: body_md -->
The probabilistic height \(H^{\text{Prob}}_{\mathbf{w},q}\), due to its logarithmic definition, takes values in the interval \([\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|,\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|+\log\max_iw_i]\). Its Dirichlet-type series is therefore a finite sum over the isotropy values. The transform of \(H^{\text{Prob}}_{\mathbf{w},q}\) used in \cref{sec:9} is instead the Laplace-type series \(\Theta_r(s)\), equivalently the mass power sum \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(s;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).
<!-- end rem-15 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
\label{def:sector}
Let \(E_\mathbf{w}\) be the set of integers \(e\ge1\), prime to \(p\), dividing at least one \(w_i\). For \(e\in E_\mathbf{w}\) put
\[
L_e := \{\mathbf{x} : x_i=0 \text{ for every } i \text{ with } e\nmid w_i\},
\qquad
X^{(e)} := X\cap L_e ,
\]
a closed subscheme of \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), and let \(\delta_e=\dim X^{(e)}\). Thus \(X^{(1)}=X\), and \(L_e\) is the fixed locus of \(\mu_e\subset\mathbb{G}_m\) acting with the weights \(\mathbf{w}\).
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:sector-qs}
Assume \(p\nmid w_i\) for all \(i\) and let \(e\in E_\mathbf{w}\) with \(X^{(e)}\neq\varnothing\). Then \(X^{(e)}\) is a weighted hypersurface, or a weighted projective space, in \(\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{w}_e}\), where \(\mathbf{w}_e\) is the subvector of \(\mathbf{w}\) indexed by \(\{i : e\mid w_i\}\); and if \(X\) is quasi-smooth, so is \(X^{(e)}\).
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The cone \(\hat X\) is stable under \(\mathbb{G}_m\), hence under \(\mu_e\), and \(\hat X\cap L_e\) is the scheme-theoretic fixed locus \(\hat X^{\mu_e}\); it is the cone over \(X^{(e)}\) inside \(L_e=\mathbb{A}^{\{i\,:\,e\mid w_i\}}\), where the equation of \(X\) restricts either to \(0\) or to a weighted homogeneous polynomial. Since \(e\mid w_i\) for some \(i\) and \(p\nmid w_i\), one has \(p\nmid e\).  After base change to \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q\), the group scheme \(\mu_e\) becomes a constant cyclic group of order \(e\).  The fixed-point scheme of a finite group of order invertible on a smooth scheme is smooth \cite[Prop.~3.4]{Edixhoven1992}.  Hence \((\hat X^{\mu_e}\setminus\{0\})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}\) is smooth, and therefore \(X^{(e)}\) is quasi-smooth.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:sector-divis}
Let \(e\in E_\mathbf{w}\), \(r\ge1\) and \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\). Then \(e\mid g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) if and only if \(\mathbf{x}\in X^{(e)}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) and \(o_e\mid r\). Consequently
\[
\Theta_r(s)=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w},\ o_e\mid r} J_{1-s}(e)\,\bigl|X^{(e)}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\bigr| .
\]
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Write \(S=S(\mathbf{x})\). One has \(e\mid g_\mathbf{x}(r)=\gcd(k_S,q^r-1)\) if and only if \(e\mid k_S\) and \(e\mid q^r-1\). The first holds if and only if \(e\mid w_i\) for every \(i\in S\), that is, \(x_i=0\) whenever \(e\nmid w_i\), that is, \(\mathbf{x}\in X^{(e)}\); the second holds if and only if \(o_e\mid r\). Since \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) is prime to \(p\), M\"obius inversion in the form \(g^{1-s}=\sum_{e\mid g}J_{1-s}(e)\) gives
\(
g_\mathbf{x}(r)^{1-s}=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}J_{1-s}(e)\,\mathbf{1}[e\mid g_\mathbf{x}(r)],
\)
and summing over \(\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) yields the displayed formula.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- rem-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:inertia-tower}
The values \(\Theta_r(1-k)\), \(k\ge0\), are the masses of a tower of stacks. Since \(\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) is the cyclic group \(\mu_{g_\mathbf{x}(r)}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\) for a twist \(\xi\) lying over \(\mathbf{x}\), any tuple of its elements commutes, so the \(k\)-fold inertia stack \(\mathbb I^k(\mathfrak X)\) of \cite{Morava-HKR}---whose objects over \(\xi\) are \(k\)-tuples \((g_1,\dots,g_k)\) in \(\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)\), with automorphism group again \(\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)\)---has
\[
\#^{\operatorname{stack}}\bigl(\mathbb I^k(\mathfrak X)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\bigr)
= \sum_{\xi\in\pi_0(\mathfrak X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))} |\operatorname{Aut}(\xi)(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|^{k-1}
= \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})} g_\mathbf{x}(r)^{k}
= \Theta_r(1-k).
\]
Because the stabilizers are abelian, the groupoid of \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\)-points of \(\mathbb I(\mathbb I^k(\mathfrak X))\) agrees, object for object, with that of \(\mathbb I^{k+1}(\mathfrak X)\), so the identity \(\Theta_r(-k)=\Theta_r(1-(k+1))\) is, in the present setting, the instance for \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb I^k(\mathfrak X)\) of the general theorem of \cite{han-park}, that the unweighted point count of any finite-type algebraic stack with quasi-separated finite-type diagonal equals the mass of its inertia stack. \cref{thm:main} packages these counts into a single two-variable formal family: for every \(k\ge0\), the specialization \(s=1-k\) is a rational function of \(t\) with Weil-type bounds inherited from the closed sectors.  No rationality assertion is made for general nonintegral \(s\).
<!-- end rem-16 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let \(X \subset \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{w}^n\) be a weighted hypersurface over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), and let \(\mathfrak{X}\) be its associated stack.
\begin{enumerate}[label={\textup{(\roman*)}}]
\item
\textup{(Sector factorization.)} The stacky height zeta function is the finite product
\[
Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak{X},s;t)
=
\prod_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}
Z\bigl(X^{(e)}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}},\,t^{\,o_e}\bigr)^{J_{1-s}(e)/o_e},
\]
over the sectors of \cref{def:sector}, with \(Z(\varnothing,t)=1\). The logarithmic derivative \(t\,\partial_t\log Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H\) is a rational function of \(t\) with at most simple poles, each satisfying
\[
t_0^{-o_e}=\alpha,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
t_0=\bigl(\zeta\,\alpha^{1/o_e}\bigr)^{-1},\quad \zeta^{o_e}=1,
\]
where \(\alpha\) is a Frobenius eigenvalue on \(H^*_c\) of the sector \(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}}\), of some integer weight \(j\) with \(0\le j\le2\dim X\). Since \(|\alpha|=q^{o_ej/2}\), this gives \(|t_0|=q^{-j/2}\); but \(t_0^{-1}\) is an \(o_e\)-th root of such an eigenvalue times a root of unity, and need not itself be a Frobenius eigenvalue of \(X\).
For \(s\in\{1,0,-1,-2,\dots\}\) the exponents \(J_{1-s}(e)/o_e\) are integers and \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak{X},s;t)\) is rational in \(t\), with
\[
Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak{X},1;t)=Z^{\operatorname{stack}}(\mathfrak{X},t)=Z(X,t),
\qquad
Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak{X},0;t)=Z^{\mathrm{tw}}(\mathfrak{X},t)=\prod_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}Z\bigl(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}},t^{o_e}\bigr)^{\phi(e)/o_e},
\]
the zeta function of the coarse space and the twist zeta function of \cite{paper-1}.

\item
Let \(\mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{w}/d\) be the reduced weight vector, and let \(\mathfrak{X}'\) be the stack of the same hypersurface in \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{w}'}\). Then
\(
Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak{X},1;t)
=
Z^{\operatorname{can}}_{H}(\mathfrak{X}',1;t),
\)
and the pushforward of the mass measure to the coarse space, the stacky height \(H^{\operatorname{stack}}\) and the stacky entropy \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{stack}}_{q^r}\)
are invariant under the common reduction \(\mathbf{w}\mapsto\mathbf{w}/d\). For \(s\neq1\) one has \(\Theta_r(s)=\Theta'_r(s)\) whenever \(\gcd(d,q^r-1)=1\), and in general the two differ by the contribution of the \(\mu_d\)-gerbe \(\mathfrak X\to\mathfrak X'\).

\item
Let \(r\) be such that \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\ne\varnothing\). The value \(\Theta_r(1)\) equals the total stacky mass \(|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\) and can be divided out to produce
\(
\Theta^{\operatorname{reg}}_r(s)
=
\Theta_r(s)/\Theta_r(1).
\)
The groupoid entropy satisfies the identity
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak{X})
=\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|
- \left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=1}
  \log \Theta^{\operatorname{reg}}_r(s),
\]
and it is the mean of the probabilistic height with respect to the mass measure.
Thus the distribution of the \(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}\)-twists by height is encoded in the behavior of the stacky height zeta function at \(s=1\).

\item
Assume in addition that \(X\) is geometrically irreducible of dimension \(n-1\ge1\). With \(\Sigma_r\), \(\varepsilon_r\), \(c_r\), \(d_X\), \(\kappa_r\), \(N_r\), and the period \(M\) of \cref{subsec:lang-weil-entropy}, one has \(\varepsilon_r=O(q^{-r})\) and \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=O(rq^{-r})\).  For \(r\) with \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\ne\varnothing\) and \(\varepsilon_r\le1/2\),
\[
h(\varepsilon_r)\le \operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)
\le h(\varepsilon_r)+\varepsilon_r\log(\kappa_r-1)
\]
when \(\kappa_r\ge2\), while the entropy is zero when \(\kappa_r=1\).  Moreover
\[
\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak X)
=\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|+\log\gcd(d_X,q^r-1)+O(q^{-rc_r}),
\]
and, whenever \(\Sigma_r\ne\varnothing\) and \(N_r\ge1\), along each residue class modulo \(M\),
\[
\varepsilon_r=N_rq^{-rc_r}\bigl(1+O(q^{-r/2})\bigr),\qquad
\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)=c_rN_r\,r\log q\,q^{-rc_r}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr).
\]
The locus \(\Sigma_r\) is determined by the non-generic rational isotropy loci \(X^\zeta\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}^\times\), \(\zeta^{d_X}\ne1\); when \(p\nmid w_i\), these are the rational non-generic twisted sectors of the inertia stack of \(\mathfrak X\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:sector-divis},
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}\Theta_r(s)\frac{t^r}{r}
=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}J_{1-s}(e)\sum_{\substack{r\ge1\\ o_e\mid r}}\bigl|X^{(e)}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\bigr|\frac{t^r}{r}
=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}\frac{J_{1-s}(e)}{o_e}\sum_{j\ge1}\bigl|X^{(e)}(\mathbb{F}_{(q^{o_e})^{j}})\bigr|\frac{(t^{o_e})^{j}}{j},
\]
where the second equality is the substitution \(r=o_ej\). The inner sum is \(\log Z(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}},t^{o_e})\), which gives the product. Each \(X^{(e)}\) is a projective variety over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), so its zeta function is rational by \cite{dwork1960}, and by the Grothendieck--Lefschetz trace formula its reciprocal zeros and poles are Frobenius eigenvalues on \(H^i_c(X^{(e)}_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q},\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\), each pure of some integer weight \(j\le i\le 2\dim X^{(e)}\le 2\dim X\) by \cite{deligne-weil2}. Substituting \(t^{o_e}\) for the variable replaces a reciprocal zero \(\alpha\) of \(Z(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}},\cdot)\) by the \(o_e\) numbers \(\zeta\alpha^{1/o_e}\), \(\zeta^{o_e}=1\), of the same absolute value, whence the statement on the poles of the logarithmic derivative.

For the integrality, \(J_k(e)\) with \(k\ge1\) is the number of elements of order exactly \(e\) in \((\mathbb{Z}/e)^k\); multiplication by \(q\) acts freely on that set with orbits of length \(o_e\), so \(o_e\mid J_k(e)\). For \(s=1\) only \(e=1\) contributes, since \(J_0(e)=0\) for \(e>1\), and the product is \(Z(X,t)\), in agreement with \cref{thm:stack-zeta}. For \(s=0\) one has \(J_1=\phi\) and \(\Theta_r(0)=\#\pi_0(\mathfrak X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}}))\), which is the definition of the twist zeta function \cite[Sec.~8.1]{paper-1}.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
At \(s=1\) the function is \(Z(X,t)\) by part (i), and the coarse varieties for \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\mathbf{w}'\) coincide. The statements on the mass measure, the stacky height and the stacky entropy are \cref{prop:mass}, \cref{prop:stack-height-inv} and \cref{prop:stack-entropy-inv}. If \(\gcd(d,q^r-1)=1\) then \(\gcd(k_S,q^r-1)=\gcd(k_S/d,q^r-1)\) for all \(S\), so \(\Theta_r=\Theta_r'\). In general the quotient \(g_S(r)/g'_S(r)\) is the local gerbe index of \cref{COR3}, computed cohomologically in \cite[Cor.~4.3]{paper-1} when \(p\nmid d\); for the hypersurface of \cref{exa:running} and \(\mathbf{w}=(2,2,4)\), \(q\) odd, one has \(\Theta'_1(0)=q+2\) and \(\Theta_1(0)=2q+\gcd(4,q-1)\).
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The sums \(\Theta_r(s)\) are recovered from the zeta function by
\(
\Theta_r(s)=\frac{1}{(r-1)!}\,\partial_t^{\,r}\log Z^{\operatorname{can}}_H(\mathfrak X,s;t)\big|_{t=0}.
\)
From the definition, \(\Theta_r(1)=\sum_\mathbf{x}1=|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\), which is the total mass by \cref{prop:mass}, and
\[
-\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=1}\log\Theta_r(s) = \frac{1}{|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})}\log g_\mathbf{x}(r).
\]
By \cref{prop:gerbe-entropy} the right-hand side is \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\operatorname{can}}_{q^r}(\mathfrak X)-\log|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|\). Equivalently, \(Z^{\operatorname{can}}(s;\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})=|X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})|^{-s}\Theta_r(s)\) and the identity is \cref{thm:duality}. The regularized sums \(\Theta_r^{\operatorname{reg}}(s)\) form the moment-generating function, in the variable \(1-s\), of the isotropy height \(\log g_\mathbf{x}(r)\) for the uniform distribution on \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\).
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The bounds for \(\operatorname{Ent}^{\text{Prob}}_{q^r}(X)\) are \cref{thm:prob-asymptotics}. For the groupoid entropy, by \cref{prop:gerbe-entropy} it suffices to estimate the mean of \(\log g_\mathbf{x}(r)\). The points outside \(\Sigma_r\) have \(g_\mathbf{x}(r)=\gcd(d_X,q^r-1)\), and the remaining points, a proportion \(\varepsilon_r\) of \(X(\mathbb{F}_{q^{r}})\), have \(1\le g_\mathbf{x}(r)\le\max_iw_i\). Hence the mean differs from \(\log\gcd(d_X,q^r-1)\) by at most \(\varepsilon_r\log\max_iw_i\). The description of \(\Sigma_r\) by the loci \(X^\zeta\) is \cref{prop:inertia}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:fe-criterion}
Let \(X\subset\mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w}\) be a weighted hypersurface over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) of dimension \(\delta\), with \(p\nmid w_i\) for all \(i\), and suppose every nonempty sector \(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}}\), \(e\in E_\mathbf{w}\), is self-dual.  If every nonempty sector has dimension \(\delta\), then for each
\[
s\in\{1,0,-1,-2,\ldots\}
\]
one has
\[
Z_H^{\operatorname{can}}\!\left(\mathfrak X,s;\frac{1}{q^{\delta}t}\right)
=\pm q^{\delta N_s/2}t^{N_s}Z_H^{\operatorname{can}}(\mathfrak X,s;t),
\qquad
N_s:=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}J_{1-s}(e)\,\chi\!\left(X^{(e)}\right).
\]
In particular, at \(s=0\),
\[
Z^{\mathrm{tw}}\!\left(\mathfrak X,\frac{1}{q^{\delta}t}\right)
=\pm q^{\delta N_0/2}t^{N_0}Z^{\mathrm{tw}}(\mathfrak X,t),
\qquad
N_0=\sum_{e\in E_\mathbf{w}}\phi(e)\,\chi\!\left(X^{(e)}\right).
\]
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Put \(Q_e=q^{o_e}\) and \(T=t^{o_e}\).  Under \(t\mapsto1/(q^{\delta}t)\), one has \(T\mapsto1/(Q_e^{\delta}T)\).  Hence the self-duality of \(X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{Q_e}\), together with \(\dim X^{(e)}=\delta\), transforms its zeta factor by
\[
Z\!\left(X^{(e)}\!\otimes\mathbb{F}_{Q_e},\frac{1}{Q_e^{\delta}T}\right)
=\pm Q_e^{\delta\chi_e/2}T^{\chi_e}
 Z\!\left(X^{(e)}\!\otimes\mathbb{F}_{Q_e},T\right).
\]
For the stated values of \(s\), the exponent \(J_{1-s}(e)/o_e\) is an integer.  Raising the preceding identity to this exponent and multiplying over \(e\) gives
\[
\sum_e\frac{J_{1-s}(e)}{o_e}\,o_e\chi_e
=\sum_eJ_{1-s}(e)\chi_e=N_s,
\]
which proves the formula.  The specialization \(s=0\) uses \(J_1=\phi\).
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:fe-exact}
Assume the hypotheses of \cref{thm:fe-criterion}, and suppose in addition that every nonempty sector is geometrically irreducible and that \(H^i_c\) of every sector is pure of weight \(i\).  Then for every fixed \(s\in\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}\), the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item every nonempty sector has dimension \(\delta\);
\item \(Z_H^{\operatorname{can}}(\mathfrak X,s;t)\) satisfies a functional equation centered at \(\delta\), of the form
\[
Z_H^{\operatorname{can}}\!\left(\mathfrak X,s;\frac{1}{q^{\delta}t}\right)
=C_s t^{N_s}Z_H^{\operatorname{can}}(\mathfrak X,s;t)
\]
for some nonzero constant \(C_s\).
\end{enumerate}
In particular, this gives a necessary and sufficient criterion for the twist zeta function at \(s=0\).
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The implication \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)} is \cref{thm:fe-criterion}.  Conversely, fix \(s\le0\).  Then \(J_{1-s}(e)>0\) for every \(e\ge1\).  For a geometrically irreducible sector \(Y=X^{(e)}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{q^{o_e}}\) of dimension \(\delta_e\), the factors coming from \(H^0_c(Y)\) give, after the substitution \(T=t^{o_e}\), a total pole multiplicity \(J_{1-s}(e)\) on the circle of reciprocal radius \(1\).  Purity prevents cancellation of these poles by odd-degree cohomology.  Likewise the top cohomology \(H^{2\delta_e}_c(Y)\) contributes total pole multiplicity \(J_{1-s}(e)\) on the circle of reciprocal radius \(q^{\delta_e}\), again without cancellation by odd-degree cohomology.

A functional equation centered at \(\delta\) carries the reciprocal-pole circle of radius \(1\) to the circle of radius \(q^{\delta}\), preserving total multiplicity.  The former receives the positive contribution \(\sum_eJ_{1-s}(e)\) from all nonempty sectors, whereas the latter receives \(\sum_{\delta_e=\delta}J_{1-s}(e)\).  Equality of these multiplicities is therefore possible only if no nonempty sector has \(\delta_e<\delta\).  Since \(X^{(1)}=X\) has dimension \(\delta\), this is exactly \textup{(i)}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- prop-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:diagonal-selfdual}
Let
\[
X=\Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^n c_ix_i^{D/w_i}=0\Bigr\}\subset\mathbb{P}^n_\mathbf{w},
\qquad c_i\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^\times,\quad w_i\mid D,\quad p\nmid D.
\]
Then every nonempty sector \(X^{(e)}\) is quasi-smooth, its \(\ell\)-adic cohomology is pure, and it is self-dual in the sense of \cref{thm:fe-criterion}.  Consequently \cref{thm:fe-criterion} applies to \(X\) whenever its nonempty sectors are equidimensional.  If, in addition, all nonempty sectors are geometrically irreducible, then \cref{cor:fe-exact} gives the converse as well.
<!-- end prop-20 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Each sector is obtained by setting to zero the coordinates outside \(\{i:e\mid w_i\}\), and the restricted equation is again diagonal.  Thus it is enough to treat \(X\).
